|last=Compston
|first=Timothy

|access-date=December 14, 2016

|archive-date=December 20, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news
|date=December 19, 2016

|archive-date=April 12, 2017}}</ref> Since 2015, it operates as an independent subsidiary of [[Canon Inc.]]<ref name="sydsvenskan-40">{{cite news

|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120404022749/http://www.securitymagazine.com/articles/securitys-25-most-influential-1
|archive-date=April 4, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news
|last=Alexandrie
|first=Lennart
|date=September 5, 2008
|title=His idea and passion was turned into a world leading industry

In the early 1990s, the company started shifting its focus away from IBM mainframes towards networking and the [[TCP/IP]] protocol. In 1991, Axis Communications introduced a multi-protocol [[print server]] supporting both TCP/IP and [[NetWare]].<ref name="axis-milestones-2009" />

In 1993, the company developed its own [[Processor design|CPU Architecture]], [[ETRAX CRIS]] (''[[Ethernet]], [[Token Ring]] Axis Code Reduced Instruction Set''), a [[RISC]] processor for use in embedded devices, with built-in support for the most common [[LAN]] technologies at the time.<ref name="axis-milestones-2009" />

In 1995, the company introduced a file-server-independent, multi-protocol [[CD-ROM]] server, supporting TCP/IP (NFS) and Windows ([[Server Message Block|SMB]]), for Ethernet networks, the AXIS 850.<ref>{{cite book
|last=Stonehouse
|first=George
|last2=Campbell
|first2=David
|last3=Hamill
|first3=Jim
|last4=Purdie
|first4=Tony
|date=2004
|title=Global and Transnational Business: Strategy and Management
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tA1bYJ8FIzIC&pg=PA333
|location=Hoboken, NJ
|publisher=John Wiley and Sons
|page=333
|isbn=0-470-85126-0}}</ref>

Sales offices were opened in [[Tokyo]], Japan in 1991, [[Hong Kong]] in 1992, and [[Singapore]] in 1995.<ref name="axis-milestones-2009" />

In 1996, Axis Communications introduced the industry's first [[network camera]], the AXIS NetEye 200.<ref>{{cite book
|last=Contos
|first=Brian
|last2=Crowell
|first2=William
|last3=Derodeff
|first3=Colby
|last4=Dunkel
|first4=Dan
|date=2007
|title=Physical and Logical Security Convergence: Powered By Enterprise Security Management
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a4h_c4TqZM4C&pg=PA65
|location=Waltham, MA
|publisher=Syngress
|page=66
|isbn=1-59749-122-5
|access-date=November 9, 2011}}</ref><ref name="infoworld-1996">{{cite news
|last=Seoane
|first=Dan
|date=November 4, 1996
|title=The Eyes have it: Microplex, Axis offer unique views
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jToEAAAAMBAJ&pg=RA1-PA35-IA5
|work=InfoWorld
|access-date=September 20, 2011}}</ref>

The introduction of this new product category came following an experimental project, where Axis engineer Carl-Axel Alm had been supervising some students building a network-based video conferencing prototype for their [[graduate thesis]]. In the end, company founder Gren saw no market for such a system at the time, but he had recently been on a business trip to Japan, where a potential network storage customer had a large stock of analog video cameras and suggested that Axis found a way to make them network-connected.<ref name="sydsvenskan-40" /><ref name="nyteknik-2024-history" />

This combination of technical experience and ideas led to the development of the network camera. The company decided that if sales exceeded 10,000 units, they would continue developing new models. 14,000 were sold. The first documented end customer was [[Steve Wozniak]]. The main early adopters were, however, oil platforms and banks.<ref name="sydsvenskan-40" /><ref name="nyteknik-2024-history" />

The possible applications of the first model were limited by its low [[frame rate]], just one every 17 seconds. To cost-efficiently improve performance, the company decided to develop its own [[system on a chip]] for video compression, the ARTPEC-1 (''Axis Real-Time Picture Encoder Chip''). It also chose to use [[Linux on embedded systems|embedded Linux]] as the [[operating system]] for the new product.<ref name="nyteknik-2024-history" /><ref name="axis-milestones-2009" /><ref name="axis-history-2026">{{cite web
|url = https://www.axis.com/about-axis/history
|title = History
|access-date = July 14, 2026
|publisher = Axis Communications AB
|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20260516203411/https://www.axis.com/about-axis/history
|archive-date = May 16, 2026
}}</ref>

In 1999, the AXIS 2100 network camera was introduced, using the new compression chip. According to the company, it was the world's first mass-produced device to use embedded Linux. For Linux to work efficiently and reliably on a device with [[Flash memory]], a new [[file system]] was needed. Therefore, the development included the creation of the file system [[JFFS]], which the company released as [[open source]] along with the new product.<ref name="axis-milestones-2009" /><ref name="axis-history-2026" /><ref>{{Cite web
|last=Amon
|first=Kyle
|date=February 28, 2001
|title=Making MPEG Movies with Axis Network Cameras {{!}} Linux Journal
|url=https://www.linuxjournal.com/article/4535
|access-date=August 21, 2020
|website=Linux Journal}}</ref>

|lang=sv

}}</ref><ref>{{cite news

In 2008, Axis Communications, together with [[Robert Bosch GmbH|Bosch]] and [[Sony]], announced that the companies would cooperate to standardize the interface of network video products and form a new industry standards body called [[ONVIF]] (Open Network Video Interface Forum).<ref name="Nine">{{cite web

|website=ONVIF (Open Network Video Interface Forum)
|access-date=November 27, 2017
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180103133405/https://www.onvif.org/pressrelease/axis-bosch-and-sony-cooperate-to-standardize-the-interface-of-network-video-products/
|archive-date=January 3, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news
|date=November 1, 2008
|title=Open Network Video Interface Forum launched
|url=http://www.securitysa.com/news.aspx?pklnewsid=30867
|work=Security Solutions
|access-date=December 11, 2014
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141219210536/http://www.securitysa.com/news.aspx?pklnewsid=30867
|archive-date=December 19, 2014}}</ref> The company's first product with ONVIF support was the AXIS P3301, launched in 2009.<ref>{{cite press release
|url = http://www.axis.com/corporate/press/industry_news/article.php?article=090921_onvif.htm

=== 2020s ===

On April 30, 2021, Axis Communications announced that it was selling Citilog, citing challenges in finding "desired synergies because of our different go-to-market models."<ref>{{cite news
|last=Honovich
|first=John
|date=April 29, 2021
|title=Axis Divests Citilog And Discontinues Demographics
|url=https://ipvm.com/reports/dis-citi-demo
|work=IPVM
|access-date=June 9, 2021}}{{subscription required
|s}}</ref>

In 2024, Axis Communications opened a research and development office for chip design in [[Stockholm, Sweden]].<ref name="nyteknik-2024-cto">{{cite news

==Operations==

Axis Communications has offices in more than 50 countries and employs around 5,000 people (average 2025). Of these, around 750 are in the Americas, around 4,000 in EMEA, and around 300 in [[Asia-Pacific]].<ref name="2025report" />

Around 18 percent of sales is invested in research and development, which is concentrated to Sweden. In Lund, where the head office is located, Axis Communications is the largest [[private-sector]] employer, with around 3,000 people in 2025. This also makes it one of the largest in all of [[Skåne County]]. === Zipstream ===
Axis Zipstream is a video compression technology introduced in 2015 for the ARTPEC-5 and later chip generations. It is designed for surveillance video and is compatible with compression standards such as H.264, H.265, and AV1. The technology adjusts compression based on image content to reduce bandwidth and storage requirements. When the technology was introduced, Axis reported an average reduction in bandwidth and storage requirements of 50%.<ref name="nyteknik-2024-cto" /><ref>{{cite web
|title = Axis Zipstream Claims Average 50% Savings
|first = Ethan
|last = Ace
|date = March 25, 2015
|work=IPVM
|url = https://ipvm.com/reports/axis-zipstream
|access-date = July 14, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|title = Reducing video storage and bandwidth by 50%
|first = Andy
|last = Clutton
|date = March 19, 2015
|url = https://www.psimagazine.co.uk/reducing-video-storage-and-bandwidth/
|access-date = October 14, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|title = CCTV Test: Dynamic Video Encoding
|url = http://benchmarkmagazine.com/cctv-test-dynamic-video-encoding/
|website = Benchmark
|date = January 24, 2017
|access-date = October 14, 2019}}</ref><ref name="ssn-zipstream-2015">{{cite news
|last=Entwistle
|first=Martha
|date=March 25, 2015
|title=Axis introduces Zipstream for more compression
|url=https://www.securitysystemsnews.com/article/axis-introduces-zipstream-more-compression
|work=Security Systems News
|access-date=July 14, 2026
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150328210017/https://www.securitysystemsnews.com/article/axis-introduces-zipstream-more-compression
|archive-date=March 28, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|title = Axis’ Zipstream technology named winner in SIA’s 2015 New Product Showcase
|work = Government Security News
|url = https://www.gsnmagazine.com/article/44435/axis%E2%80%99_zipstream_technology_named_winner_sia%E2%80%99s_2015
|access-date = October 14, 2019
|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190420163158/https://www.gsnmagazine.com/article/44435/axis%E2%80%99_zipstream_technology_named_winner_sia%E2%80%99s_2015
|archive-date = April 20, 2019}}</ref>

Zipstream analyzes and adjusts the video stream in real time using concepts such as Region of Interest (ROI) and Group of Pictures (GOP). Areas containing details such as faces and license plates are assigned higher image quality, while lower-priority areas such as walls and vegetation can be compressed more heavily. Later updates added support for PTZ camera movements and frame-rate-based adjustments to the video stream bit rate.<ref>{{cite news

=== Microprocessors ===
The Axis Real-Time Picture Encoder Chip (ARTPEC) is a system on a chip ([[System on a chip|SoC]]) developed by Axis Communications.<ref>{{Cite web
|last=Viklund
|first=Lars
|title=Introduction to Hardware Verification
|url=https://www.isy.liu.se/edu/kurs/TSEA44/forelasning/Introduction_to_Hardware_Verification.pdf}}</ref> There are currently nine generations of the chip, all of which run AXIS OS, a modified version of [[Linux]] designed for [[Embedded system|embedded devices]]. Not all products developed by Axis Communications use its custom chip. == Cybersecurity vulnerabilities ==

In July 2017, cyber security researchers found a vulnerability in the [[gSOAP]] code library. All ONVIF-compatible products were affected, including those produced by Axis Communications.<ref>{{cite news
|title = "Devil's Ivy" Vulnerability Could Hit Millions of IoT Devices
|first = Andy
|last = Greenberg
|date = July 18, 2017
|url = https://www.wired.com/story/devils-ivy-iot-vulnerability/
|newspaper = Wired
|access-date = October 14, 2019
|issn=1059-1028}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|title = Experts in Lather Over ‘gSOAP’ Security Flaw

|url = https://krebsonsecurity.com/2017/07/experts-in-lather-over-gsoap-security-flaw/
|date = July 18, 2017
|access-date = October 14, 2019}}</ref>

In October 2021, cybersecurity research firm Nozomi Networks published "three new vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-31986, CVE-2021-31987, CVE-2021-31988) affecting all Axis devices based on the embedded AXIS OS." Axis and Nozomi collaborated throughout the research and disclosure process.<ref name="Nozomi">{{cite web
